subject: Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling

messages.author: f8a4136bfeaed71c
messages.subject: Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling
parts:
Hi all,

We all know that running a confirmatory factor analysis model in Stan when it has a unique solution will obtain the solutions up to the sign. For example in the trace plot (attached file) when fitting a FA model with one common factor, we get two solutions (uniqueness up to the sign). I do not want to set the sign when fitting the model by <lower=0> or <upper=0>. I let Stan do what it should do because in the case when a factor loading is close to 0, we could see it crosses 0.

However, when we got the chains as in the trace plots, then posterior summary makes no sense. So after running this:

model1 = stan(file="model1.stan", data = data1,
              iter=1000, chains = 3,
              pars = c('lambda', 'sigma', 'xi'))

I would like to have something like

'sign(model1$chain3$lambda)=-1'

'joint=join(chain1, chain2, chain3.new)' and I can derive posterior from 'joint'. (I put in quote because that is what I want but of course not valid in R or Rstan).


Thank you for your help!

Kind regards,
Tran.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling
parts: Hi Tran,

On Mon, Feb 13, 2017 at 9:09 AM, Dung Tran <trungd...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Daniel,

Thank you for your answer, but that I think a strong prior for example when the factor loading is close to 0 but that prior brings it back to 0.5.
That's fine, but you can still take a weak prior that's not symmetric.
So just let Stan sample with vague priors and I would like to do something after having posteriors. I would just change the sign of some chains.

Fundamentally, that's not what you should do. It's not really Bayesian: the goal is to get the posterior distribution. When you see the modes separate across chains and you don't want to change your model, the right thing to do is either change the model (all you need is a little structure to break exchangeability) or run until you see hairy caterpillars. Although, I don't know what you'd gain if the expectation is 0, and you have two very strongly identified modes that are symmetric around 0.

Want to try putting a prior down first?


Daniel

Tran.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling
parts:
Coincidentally I’ve been working on a case study for a similar problem
so I can offer a warning that an asymmetric prior is unlikely to help
unless it is _extremely_ informative.  It’s really hard to overwhelm the
likelihood sufficiently to suppress that second mode.

But more importantly you don’t actually want to end up “averaging 
around zero” if the effect is small.  That is actually a somewhat artificial 
consequence of having a degenerate likelihood — in particular while
the mean might seem like it’s giving the correct answer, the variance
will be inflated.

A cute narrative that may help build intuition is to think about this as
a decision problem.  You are a robot with an obstacle in front of you
so you can turn towards the left or right to avoid the obstacle, but if
you average over the entire posterior you end up going forwards and
crashing into the obstacle!  

Anyways, setting a positivity constraint will give you the posterior 
inferences that you want.  When the effect size is small the posterior
will concentrate towards zero and you can judge the magnitude of
it’s effect with posterior probabilities like P[effect < threshold] for some
application-specific threshold.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling
parts:
Hi all,

You could see the difference in the attached figures for the trace plot of lambda[5]. By simulation the true value of lambda[5] is 0. The first figure (without constraint) shows that point because we see the trace plot crossing 0 (CI contains 0) but when we set positive constraint, we do not see that.

So I think putting positive constraints might give misleading inference when we do not know the true values.

Tran.

On 13 February 2017 at 15:54, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
Coincidentally I’ve been working on a case study for a similar problem
so I can offer a warning that an asymmetric prior is unlikely to help
unless it is _extremely_ informative.  It’s really hard to overwhelm the
likelihood sufficiently to suppress that second mode.

But more importantly you don’t actually want to end up “averaging 
around zero” if the effect is small.  That is actually a somewhat artificial 
consequence of having a degenerate likelihood — in particular while
the mean might seem like it’s giving the correct answer, the variance
will be inflated.

A cute narrative that may help build intuition is to think about this as
a decision problem.  You are a robot with an obstacle in front of you
so you can turn towards the left or right to avoid the obstacle, but if
you average over the entire posterior you end up going forwards and
crashing into the obstacle!  

Anyways, setting a positivity constraint will give you the posterior 
inferences that you want.  When the effect size is small the posterior
will concentrate towards zero and you can judge the magnitude of
it’s effect with posterior probabilities like P[effect < threshold] for some
application-specific threshold.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Change the sign of some chains after posterior sampling
parts:
Tran,

Again, I have to argue that the positive-constrained chains are 
more correct.  In the unconstrained case you’re not crossing
zero because zero is the true value, you’re crossing it because
you’re adjoining two symmetric distributions together.  For
example, if the true effect size was small but non-zero then the 
posterior would look multimodal with a bridge connected the
modes across the zero.  Markov chains would cross zero over
and over again transitioning between the two modes, but that
doesn’t mean that the true effect size is zero!  In other words,
zero-crossings does not imply zero effect size and vice versa.

If you looked at the marginal posterior for lambda[5] in the
positive-constrained and identified case you’d see that it
concentrates towards zero, informing that the effect size is
small and possibly zero which is about all you can say with
finite data.

-Mike

I agree with Mike, and I think he explained this very well.

If you don't know how to choose the application specific threshold, you could run your model with permuted data (so that there is no effect, but the amount of data and marginal distributions of data are same) and look at the posterior in the case where you know there is no effect.
